t.ilha comprida wild life zone@-24.9,-47.7:
Ilha Comprida, the long island, is exactly what its name promises: a narrow barrier island of sand, dunes and restinga scrub that runs for roughly seventy kilometres along the southern coast of São Paulo state, separating the Atlantic from the calm inland waters of the Mar Pequeno. Behind it lies the Lagamar, one of the largest estuarine complexes in Brazil, a maze of channels, mangroves and islands stretching south toward Cananéia and Paranaguá. This entire region, including the Ilha Comprida protected areas, forms part of the Atlantic Forest South-East Reserves, listed by UNESCO in 1999 for preserving one of the richest and most threatened ecosystems on Earth.

Nature is the star here. The mangroves are nurseries for fish, crabs and shrimp, and the channels are home to a resident population of Guiana dolphins, often seen near Cananéia. Scarlet ibises, herons and the endemic red-tailed parrot live in the forests and wetlands, and sea turtles feed along the coast. Inland, the Serra do Mar mountains rise steeply, covered in dense forest, with waterfalls and caves.

The history goes back a long way too. Cananéia claims to be one of the oldest settlements in Brazil, founded in the early sixteenth century, and Iguape, across the bridge from the northern tip of the island, has a beautiful colonial centre and the sanctuary of Bom Jesus de Iguape, which draws thousands of pilgrims every August. A canal dug in the nineteenth century to connect the Ribeira river to the port of Iguape grew far wider than intended and changed the salinity of the estuary, a cautionary tale still told by local fishermen.

The main access is the BR-116, the busy highway between São Paulo and Curitiba, followed by smaller roads through banana plantations and forest down to the coast. These roads are mostly flat and straight, with some curves near the hills. Rain is frequent and heavy, especially in summer, and the humidity is high. Iguape, about twenty-six kilometres away, and Pariquera-Açu have fuel and supermarkets. Try the local seafood, especially oysters from Cananéia, and a pastel de camarão, a fried pastry stuffed with shrimp.
t.serra do itapitangui@-24.9,-48.0:
The Serra do Itapitangui rises behind Cananéia, on the southern coast of São Paulo state, a modest coastal range covered in dense Atlantic Forest that looks down on one of the best-preserved estuaries in Brazil. The forest here is part of the Atlantic Forest South-East Reserves, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999, which protects a vast area of forest, mangroves and coastal islands stretching from São Paulo into Paraná. The Mata Atlântica once covered much of Brazil's coast; today, only a fraction remains, and this region holds some of the largest and best-preserved stretches.

The forest is a riot of life: giant trees draped with bromeliads, orchids and lianas, palms, tree ferns and countless species of birds, butterflies and frogs. Toucans, parrots and tanagers flash through the canopy, and if you are lucky you might see a howler monkey or a capuchin. From the hills, the views over the estuary, the channels, the mangroves and the islands are spectacular, especially at sunset.

Cananéia, at the foot of the hills, is one of the oldest towns in Brazil, with a small historic centre of colonial houses and churches. It is the gateway to the Ilha do Cardoso State Park, an island of forest, beaches and traditional fishing communities, reached by boat. The estuary is a nursery for fish and shellfish, and Cananéia is famous for its oysters, farmed in the mangroves and served fresh or grilled in the restaurants along the waterfront.

The riding is relaxed. The road to Cananéia from the BR-116 runs through farmland and forest, with some curves and hills, and the roads around the town are quiet, with views of the water and the mangroves. The climate is hot and humid, with heavy rain in summer, so be ready for downpours and slippery roads. Cananéia, about twelve kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Cajati and Jacupiranga, inland, are larger towns on the highway. Try oysters with lime, fried fish with rice and beans, or a moqueca, a fish stew with coconut milk and palm oil.
t.the chatkal state biosphere nature reser:
East of Tashkent, the Western Tian Shan rises in a series of ridges, and the Chatkal range is one of the most accessible of them, its snowy peaks visible from the capital on a clear day. The Chatkal State Biosphere Reserve protects a part of this landscape, with forests of juniper, walnut, maple and wild fruit trees, and alpine meadows above, home to Tian Shan brown bears, snow leopards, ibex, wild boar and many birds of prey. The Western Tian Shan, shared by Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, is on the UNESCO list.

The area is rich in wild fruit trees, including apples, apricots, pistachios and walnuts, many of them ancestors of cultivated varieties. In spring, the slopes are covered with wildflowers, including tulips, and in autumn the forests turn gold. Access to the reserve itself is restricted, and permits are needed, but the valleys around the edges offer plenty of walking, and shepherds with flocks on the high pastures are usually happy to point the way.

The road from Tashkent to the Fergana valley, the A373, crosses the Kamchik pass at about 2,270 metres, a spectacular route through the mountains, with tunnels, hairpins and views over the Angren valley. It is a busy road, with trucks, buses and checkpoints, so take care. The pass can be closed in winter due to snow. Nearby, the Chimgan and Beldersay mountain resorts and the Charvak reservoir are popular weekend escapes for Tashkent residents.

Angren, a coal-mining town of over one hundred thousand, and Yangiobod are the nearest larger towns, with fuel and services. Fuel quality and availability in Uzbekistan can vary, and many cars run on gas, so fill up when you can. Try plov, the national rice dish, shashlik, samsa and fresh fruit from roadside stalls. The best times to visit are spring and autumn, when the weather is mild and the colours are at their most vivid.
t.sairam ugam state national nature park b:
In the south of Kazakhstan, where the western spurs of the Tien Shan rise from the steppe, the Sairam-Ugam National Park protects a landscape of high mountains, deep valleys, juniper forests and alpine meadows. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Western Tien Shan, shared between Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, recognised for its exceptional biodiversity, including wild relatives of fruit trees such as apples, pears and walnuts, which are believed to be the ancestors of many cultivated varieties.

The park is home to snow leopards, brown bears, ibex and argali, the wild mountain sheep, as well as many birds of prey. In spring, the meadows are covered with wild tulips, including species that are ancestors of the garden tulips of the Netherlands. The mountains rise to over four thousand metres, and the rivers, such as the Ugam, flow through deep gorges. The park has trails for walking and horse riding, and guesthouses in the villages offer accommodation.

The riding to the park is from Shymkent, the main city of southern Kazakhstan, through the town of Lenger and into the foothills. The roads are paved on the main routes but become rough and unpaved as you climb into the mountains. Traffic is light, but livestock on the roads is common. The climate is continental, with hot summers and cold winters, and the mountains can be snowy until late spring. The best time to visit is from May to September. Some areas of the park require permits, so check before you go.

Lenger, about twenty-seven kilometres away, is a town with fuel and basic services, and Shymkent has all services. Fuel in Kazakhstan is generally cheap and available. Kazakh food includes beshbarmak, boiled meat with noodles, plov and kumis, fermented mare's milk, an acquired taste. The villages in the foothills offer homestays where you can experience local life. Riding into the mountains in spring, with the tulips in bloom and the snowy peaks above, is an unforgettable experience.
t.jacupiranga state park@-24.9,-48.3:
The Vale do Ribeira, in the far south of São Paulo state, holds the largest continuous remnant of Atlantic Forest left in Brazil, and the Jacupiranga area, near the border with Paraná, is part of that green expanse. The Atlantic Forest once covered much of Brazil's coast, but centuries of logging, farming and urban growth reduced it to a fraction of its former extent, and what remains here, together with neighbouring reserves, forms part of the UNESCO site of the Atlantic Forest Southeast Reserves, inscribed in 1999. The forest is incredibly rich in species, with jaguars, pumas, monkeys, toucans and countless orchids and bromeliads.

The original Jacupiranga State Park, created in 1969, was reorganised in 2008 into a mosaic of protected areas, including state parks, sustainable development reserves and areas for traditional communities, recognising the presence of quilombola communities, descendants of escaped slaves, and others who have lived in the region for generations. The landscape is a maze of mountains, rivers and limestone caves, some of which are open to visitors in nearby parks, with stalactites and underground rivers.

Riding here is an adventure. The BR-116, the Régis Bittencourt highway linking São Paulo and Curitiba, passes through the region, with heavy truck traffic and a history of dangerous stretches through the Serra do Cafezal, now largely duplicated. Off the highway, the roads into the Ribeira valley are narrower, winding through forested hills, banana plantations and small towns, with many curves and some steep sections. Unpaved roads are common, and heavy tropical rain can turn them to mud quickly. The best riding season is the drier winter months, from May to September.

Cajati, about twenty-six kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel, shops and restaurants, and Jacupiranga and Registro offer more services along the highway. Food in the region is simple and hearty, with rice, beans, grilled meats and plenty of bananas, which are the main crop of the valley. Carry water and rain gear, because the weather can change quickly. Stop at a forest edge or by a river, and listen to the birds and insects. The Atlantic Forest is one of the most threatened ecosystems on earth, and seeing it alive and wild is a privilege.
t.besh aral state nature reserve main part:
Far up the Chatkal valley in western Kyrgyzstan, where the river runs between the Chatkal and Sandalash ranges of the Western Tien Shan, lies the Besh-Aral State Nature Reserve. It protects mountain steppe, juniper woodland, walnut and apple groves and rocky high country, and it is part of the transnational World Heritage Site of the Western Tien Shan, inscribed in 2016 and shared with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. The reserve was created in particular to protect Menzbier's marmot, a small marmot found only in this part of Central Asia.

The Chatkal valley is remote even by Kyrgyz standards. It is cut off from the rest of the country by high passes, and for much of the year the only road access is over a pass that is closed by snow in winter. The few villages in the valley live from herding, farming and, increasingly, gold mining. The landscape is wild and beautiful: green valleys, snowy peaks, rushing rivers and wide open spaces with yurts in summer.

Getting there is a serious undertaking. The roads into the Chatkal are mostly gravel and dirt, with steep climbs, hairpins, river crossings and rockfall. The passes are high, above 3,000 metres, and weather can change quickly, with snow possible even in summer. The season is short: roughly from June to September, the passes are usually open, but check locally before setting out. A dual-sport bike, good tyres and a reliable tool kit are essential.

Within the reserve, access may require permission, and some areas are strictly protected. Wildlife includes snow leopards, ibex, argali, bears and many birds of prey, though most are shy and hard to see. The marmots are easier: listen for their whistles and look for them standing guard by their burrows.

Fuel and services are very limited in the Chatkal. Carry enough fuel for long distances, plus spare, and be prepared to buy petrol from local sellers in bottles. Food and accommodation are available in homestays in some villages, where you will be offered bread, tea, kumis, fermented mare's milk, and meat. The hospitality is genuine, and the experience of riding through such a remote valley is one of the great adventures of Central Asia.
t.besh aral state nature reserve shandalas:
This is a remote place, and I should say so plainly. The coordinates fall in the high country of the western Tien Shan, near the point where Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan crowd together, and the label belongs to the Besh-Aral State Nature Reserve, a protected area created in the late twentieth century to guard mountain forest and meadow along the Talas and Chatkal ranges. I do not know a particular feature called Shandalas well enough to describe it, so what follows is about the landscape around it, not a guided tour.

The reserve protects a range of habitats from dry foothills to juniper and spruce forest, up through alpine meadow to bare rock and snow. Wildlife includes brown bear, ibex and the elusive snow leopard, along with marmots in the meadows and golden eagles overhead. The Tien Shan, whose name means the Celestial Mountains, is one of the great Asian ranges, and even in its western outliers the scale is hard to take in: ridges stacked behind ridges, rivers cutting deep gorges, and walnut forests in the lower valleys that have been harvested for centuries.

For a motorcyclist, this is adventure country rather than touring country. Roads in the surrounding districts range from reasonable asphalt in the valleys to rutted gravel and river crossings in the hills, and weather can change in an hour from hot sunshine to cold rain or snow. There are no towns listed nearby, which tells you everything about the fuel and food situation: nothing is guaranteed, so carry fuel, water, a repair kit and a means of calling for help. Access to protected areas, border zones and some high passes may require permits, so check locally before you go, and go with another rider rather than alone.

The best season is June to September, when the passes are usually clear and the meadows are in flower, with the clearest views in the cooler days of early autumn. In the evening the valleys fill with the smell of juniper smoke and sheep, and the stars are extraordinarily bright. If you reach this place, you have earned it, and the right response is to ride out again carefully.
t.intervales state park@-24.3,-48.3:
There is a place in the hills of south-east São Paulo state where you can hear a monkey you will probably never see. The muriqui, the largest primate in the Americas, lives in the Atlantic Forest of the Serra de Paranapiacaba, and Intervales State Park, one of the largest protected areas of that forest, is one of its refuges. The park covers more than forty thousand hectares of steep, misty hills, with giant ferns, bromeliads, orchids and trees hung with vines, and it is part of the Atlantic Forest South-East Reserves, listed by UNESCO in 1999. Toucans, tapirs and, rarely, jaguars share it.

Under the forest, the limestone has dissolved into caves, some of them open to visitors with a guide, with cool air, dripping water and formations. The park runs as an ecotourism area, with trails, birdwatching hides and simple lodging, so you can stay for a night or two. In the morning, mist rises from the trees, and the sound of birds is almost deafening.

Capão Bonito, a town of about thirty-seven thousand, is the gateway, with fuel, shops and restaurants, and it is the last reliable place to tank up. From there, the road to the park is a long one, with a stretch of unpaved track through farmland and forest, with red clay that turns into a slick, sticky mess in rain. Dry weather makes it a fine, dusty ride, but a heavy storm can close it, so ask at the town or the park office. The paved approach roads from Sorocaba and São Paulo are busy with trucks, with a lot of curves and fog on the higher parts.

The best season is the drier months, April to September, when the days are cool and the trails are firm. Summers are warm and wet, with sudden downpours. Bring layers, because mornings are cold, and insect repellent for the evenings. Try a plate of rice and beans with fried banana in a country restaurant, a strong coffee and a slice of corn cake, and give yourself time, because the forest does not hurry.
t.lauraceas state park@-24.2,-48.0:
The Vale do Ribeira is one of the least developed regions of São Paulo state, a long valley of banana plantations, tea fields, small towns and thick forest, with a river that runs unimpeded to the sea. Because it was never heavily built up, it holds the largest remaining block of Atlantic Forest in Brazil, and the state parks of the area, among them Lauráceas, protect it. The name refers to the laurel family, which includes trees such as canelas and sassafras that grow tall in the damp forest, and which give the park its scent of spice when the wind moves the leaves.

Registro, a town of about forty-five thousand, is the main centre of the valley, and it has a story that surprises visitors. It was settled by Japanese immigrants in the early twentieth century, who established tea plantations and rice fields, and their descendants still hold festivals, with taiko drums, food stalls and a Japanese garden. Capão Bonito, to the north, is the other gateway, and both have fuel and services.

The park itself is a place for walkers and wildlife, and access is limited, so ask at the local office about permission and conditions. The roads in the valley are a mix of paved main routes and dirt tracks, with heavy rains turning them to mud for days, and fuel is harder to find in the villages than on the main roads. The famous BR-116, the Régis Bittencourt highway, runs through here, linking São Paulo and Curitiba, and is known for its curves, heavy lorries and fog on the Serra do Cafezal, so take extra care and avoid it at night.

Quilombo communities, descended from escaped slaves, still live in the valley, farming and preserving their traditions, and some offer visits and meals. Try palm heart, fish from the river and banana sweets, and ask politely before photographing people. The cooler months from May to September are comfortable, and summers are hot, humid and thunderous. Bring rain gear in any season, because the forest makes its own weather.
t.padysha ata state nature reserve@41.7,71:
In the far west of Kyrgyzstan, where the Chatkal range runs along the edge of the Fergana valley and the border with Uzbekistan, a steep, forested set of mountains shelters the Padysha-Ata reserve. It is a strictly protected nature area, one of several state reserves in the country, and its purpose is the plain business of keeping a piece of the western Tian Shan as it was. The slopes carry forest and mountain meadow, rivers rush down from snowfields, and the peaks above are high enough to carry glaciers.

I should be honest about what I know. This is a remote place, and not one with a large visitor infrastructure, and details like access, permits and trails change from year to year. Strict nature reserves in Kyrgyzstan often require permission, and areas near the border are sometimes restricted, so arrange it before you go, ideally through a local community-based tourism office or a guide. Do not plan to ride into the reserve itself, because the point of such a place is that vehicles stay outside.

The surrounding country is superb riding, if you are prepared. The roads in southern Kyrgyzstan wind along river valleys and over high passes, with surfaces that range from good asphalt to broken gravel, and landslides and washouts are possible after rain. Distances are long, towns are few, and the altitude gives you cold nights even in summer. Shepherds move their flocks to high pastures, the jailoo, in summer, and yurts appear on the green slopes, where hospitality is a matter of honour. Accept a bowl of kymyz, the fermented mare's milk, if you dare, and fresh bread with cream.

The nearest town is Kerben, about thirty kilometres away, with a few shops and basic fuel, and larger services are in Jalal-Abad, a long drive away. Carry spare fuel, water, tools and some cash in som, since cards are not widely accepted. Summer, from June to September, is the only sensible season for the high roads, and autumn brings crisp air and golden walnut and poplar trees in the valleys.
t.alto ribeira touristic state park@-24.5,:
The Ribeira valley, in the south of Sao Paulo state, holds the largest remaining stretch of Atlantic Forest in Brazil, and under it lies one of the great cave regions of the Americas. The park called PETAR, the Alto Ribeira Touristic State Park, covers hills of limestone that are riddled with hundreds of caves, many of them with underground rivers, huge chambers and elaborate formations of stalactites and stalagmites. The forest above is thick with ferns, bromeliads and trees draped in moss, and it belongs to the Atlantic Forest South-East Reserves, a UNESCO World Heritage listing from 1999.

The caves are the main attraction, and several can be visited by anyone with a guide. Casa de Pedra, the House of Stone, has one of the largest cave entrances in the world, a huge arch of rock some two hundred metres high, and Santana cave is known for its beautiful formations. Others have waterfalls, subterranean streams and colonies of bats. Guides are required, and the rules about helmets, lamps and group sizes are strictly applied, so arrange a visit through the park's offices or a local operator. The forest above has jaguars and tapirs, though sightings are extremely rare, and many kinds of birds.

The roads of this region are fine riding, though it is one of the poorer parts of the state, with small villages and long stretches of forest. The highway from Apiai towards Iporanga winds through hills with bends, steep sections and some patched surfaces, and in the wet season, from December to March, heavy rain can cause landslides and make unpaved side roads slippery. The dry months, from April to September, are cooler and safer. Mist often lies in the valleys in the morning, and the air is rich with the smell of damp earth and leaves.

Apiai, seventeen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and is the best base. Villages inside the park area have small guesthouses and simple food, with rice, beans, manioc and river fish. Carry water, insect repellent and a light waterproof, and wear sturdy shoes for the cave floors, which can be wet and slippery. The local people are welcoming and used to travellers.
t.xitue ecological station@-24.3,-48.3:
The Xitue Ecological Station is a different kind of place from most on a route map, because it is not for visitors. It is a strictly protected reserve in the interior of Sao Paulo state, set aside for scientific research and conservation, and normal tourism is not allowed. It forms part of the Atlantic Forest South-East Reserves, the UNESCO listing that protects what is left of a forest that once covered the whole Brazilian coast and has been reduced to a small fraction of its former extent. Its role is to keep a piece of that forest intact, as a reference and a refuge for animals and plants that cannot survive elsewhere.

What you can do is ride around it, and appreciate it from the outside. The roads of the region run through a mosaic of forest remnants, pastures, eucalyptus plantations and small farms, and the contrast between the dense, dark green of the protected forest and the more open land around it is striking. In the mornings, mist rises from the valleys, and the calls of birds, including toucans and parrots, come from the edge of the trees. The area lies in the upper basin of the Paranapanema and the Ribeira valleys, and the climate is humid, with frequent rain.

Roads vary from good asphalt to dirt tracks that turn to red mud after storms, so check the weather before setting out. Gradients are moderate, bends are frequent and the scenery changes with each ridge. Traffic is mostly trucks, farm vehicles and the occasional bus. The best months for riding are from April to September, when it is drier and cooler, and the summer months bring heavy downpours, which can cause floods and landslides. Respect fences and signs, and do not try to enter the reserve.

Capao Bonito, about thirty kilometres away, is the main town of the area, with fuel, shops and a cluster of restaurants, and it is where you should fill up and stock up. Villages nearer the reserve have little. Enjoy a plate of rice, beans and grilled meat in a roadside restaurant, and a strong Brazilian coffee, which is excellent. The people of the region are friendly and happy to help with directions.
t.aksu jabagly state nature reserve aulie@:
Aulie is a Kazakh word, borrowed from Arabic, that means holy or saintly, and it attaches to many places in the steppe where a shrine, a spring or a grave has drawn pilgrims for centuries. At the northern edge of the Aksu-Jabagly reserve, thirty kilometres from the village of Bayzhansay, the name marks the second of the reserve's approaches, and it opens onto a quieter side of the Talas Alatau, where the foothills climb through juniper and wild apple toward bare grey summits.

Wild apples and walnuts are a quiet claim to fame in this part of the Tien Shan, a region often named as the ancestral home of the cultivated apple. The wild apple forests of the mountains still hold trees with fruit of every shape and size, and the genetic diversity that survives in places like this has been a resource for breeders for a century. In autumn, the slopes smell of fermenting fruit, and bears come down to feed, which is a good reason to keep voices up on a walk.

Local life is pastoral. Families move their herds of horses, sheep and cattle up to summer pastures in June and bring them down in September, and you will see felt yurts, smoke rising from small fires and young riders on horseback. If you meet herders, greetings are formal, with a handshake and a question about the health of the herd, and an invitation to tea is not to be refused lightly. Fermented mare's milk, kumis, is drunk in summer, and the first taste is an acquired one.

Roads in this region are poor. Tracks to the reserve cross streams and loose stones, turn to mud after rain and may be blocked by snow or rockfall. Distances are long and phone signals are weak, so tell someone your route, and take spare fuel, a tow rope and a repair kit. The nearest town with reliable fuel is far away, and the larger city of Shymkent is the place to stock up. A permit is needed for the reserve and the border zone.

Late spring and early summer bring wildflowers, and September has crisp air, golden light and ripe fruit.
t.carlos botelho state park@-24.2,-48.0:
Carlos Botelho State Park protects a big piece of the Atlantic Forest on the slopes of the Serra de Paranapiacaba, in the south of São Paulo state, and it is one of the best remaining pieces of a forest that once covered the whole coast of Brazil. Less than a tenth of the original Atlantic Forest survives, and what is left is crowded with life: tapirs, ocelots, the occasional jaguar, hundreds of bird species and the muriqui, the woolly spider monkey, the largest primate in the Americas. The park is among the few places where this endangered monkey still lives.

The forest is dense, damp and layered, with giant trees draped in epiphytes, tree ferns in the understorey and palm trees whose heart is a favourite food of local people. Mist rolls in from the coast, rain is frequent, and the air smells of wet earth and leaf mould. A state road crosses the park, and on that stretch the experience of riding is unusual: a quiet, winding road through walls of green, with patches of fog, wet tarmac, and the sudden calls of birds. Toucans, tanagers and trogons are all possible, and at dawn the forest is loud. Wildlife can wander onto the road, so keep your speed down, particularly in the early morning and at dusk.

Services are limited. Juquiá, about thirty-eight kilometres away with thirteen thousand people, is the nearest town of size, and fuel and food should be arranged there or in the larger towns of the Ribeira valley. The park has a visitor centre and trails, some of them short and easy, others long and demanding. Bring insect repellent, long sleeves and a rain jacket, because ticks, mosquitoes and downpours are all part of the deal.

The road surface varies from good to broken, and heavy rain can cause landslides on slopes. The wet season runs from roughly October to March, and the drier months of May to September are more comfortable for riding, though mist and drizzle are possible all year. UNESCO lists the park as part of the Atlantic Forest South-East Reserves. Respect the signs, keep to marked trails, and take your litter away. The reward is a landscape that feels, in the early morning with mist in the canopy, like something very old.
t.jureia itatins ecological station@-24.4,:
Jureia-Itatins is a rare piece of coast. Between the sea and the Serra dos Itatins, in the south of São Paulo state, a long stretch of Atlantic Forest runs down to the beach with few roads and almost no development, and the ecological station that protects it is one of the largest remaining blocks of coastal forest in the state. The land rises from white sand and mangrove to wet forest on the ridges, with rivers running out through the trees to the sea, and the whole thing is so thick and green that satellite pictures show it as a dark patch among the paler towns.

The reserve is strictly protected, and most of it is closed to ordinary visitors, with entry only for research and for managed access to some areas. That is the point. Fishing communities, the caiçaras, have lived on this coast for centuries, mixing Indigenous, Portuguese and African traditions, and their way of life, with cassava flour, fishing canoes and their own songs, is part of the story of the place. Peruíbe, the nearest town, is a seaside resort of about sixty thousand people, known for the black mud of its river, which locals say has healing properties, and for a long beach and a quiet, old-fashioned feel.

Riding here is a matter of finding the roads that touch the edge. The coast road from Peruíbe runs through a mix of town, beach settlement and forest, with some bends and mostly good surface, and on the way you pass banana plantations and small farms. Beach access roads are narrow, often sandy, and prone to flooding. A trip to the beach at Guaraú, where a river falls over the rocks toward the sea, is a standard excursion. The weather is warm and humid for most of the year, rain falls heavily in summer, and the cooler months of May to September are best.

Fuel is easy in Peruíbe, which has stations, shops and restaurants. Fish is fresh, with moqueca, a stew of fish, coconut milk and palm oil, the dish to try. Carry sun cream, repellent and a rain layer, and keep the bike away from salt spray when you can. Respect the park boundaries and rules, because enforcement is real, and the forest is far more valuable standing than as a short cut.
The Atlantic Forest South-East Reserves are not one place but a scatter of about two dozen protected areas in the south of São Paulo state and the north of Paraná, recognised by UNESCO as a single World Heritage property because together they hold one of the biggest remaining tracts of Atlantic Forest. The pin falls in the hills above the Ribeira de Iguape valley, a region known as the Vale do Ribeira, which is both the poorest part of the state and the one with the most forest left. Poverty and forest have an odd relationship: the lack of big roads and industry is exactly what kept the trees standing.

The valley has its own history. The Ribeira river flows for hundreds of kilometres without a dam on its main course, and gold was panned along it in colonial times. In the early twentieth century, Japanese immigrants settled in the area around Registro and began growing tea, and tea is still grown there, with neat green rows on the hillsides and a small town with a distinctly Japanese influence in its festivals and its food. Banana plantations cover the flat lands, and old caves in the limestone hills nearby hold stalactites and underground rivers.

For a rider, the region is a place for quiet roads and long views of green. The main highway through the valley is a busy two-lane road with trucks and buses, and tropical rain is a recurring hazard, but the side roads climb into wet forest and run through small farms. Surfaces are variable, with sections of broken asphalt and patches of dirt, and mist makes visibility poor in the early hours. Ticks, mosquitoes and leeches live in the undergrowth, so keep to the paths when you stop. The dry season from May to September is better for riding, and the summer rains can last for days.

Registro, about thirty-nine kilometres away with forty-five thousand people, is the sensible place for fuel, food and a bed. Try the tea, the bananas, and the Japanese-influenced dishes sold in small restaurants, and ask about local festivals, which can fill the town for a weekend. Bring a rain jacket at any time of year, carry water and spare food on the bike, and make a note of the nearest fuel before you leave the highway. In such a green and empty region, it is easy to run low on all three.
t.ilhabela ferry@-23.8,-45.4:
The ferry from São Sebastião to Ilhabela is a short crossing of about fifteen minutes across a narrow channel, and it is the only way for vehicles to reach the island. Ilhabela, the largest sea island in Brazil, is a steep, forested mountain rising out of the Atlantic, with beaches, waterfalls and a handful of villages scattered around its shore. The mainland side is São Sebastião, a port town of over seventy-five thousand people with a historic centre of colonial churches and a working harbour.

The Rio-Santos Highway, which runs along this part of the São Paulo coast, is a famous road, with rolling bends, jungle-covered slopes dropping to the sea, and hidden beaches. It runs between the Serra do Mar, the mountain range that rises behind the coast, and the ocean, and the Atlantic Forest, one of the most diverse and threatened ecosystems on the planet, clings to every slope. The road is generally well surfaced, but heavy rain can cause landslides, and in holiday periods traffic can be extremely slow.

For riders, the ferry is a fun and sometimes frustrating part of the journey. Queues can be long on weekends and in summer, with a wait of an hour or more, so arrive early or on a weekday. Motorcycles are generally loaded first or squeezed in, and the crew will guide you. Keep your documents handy and have cash for the fare.

São Sebastião has fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and Caraguatatuba, about twenty kilometres south-west, is larger and has more services. On the island, fuel is available but more expensive. Remember that biting flies, called borrachudos, are active at dusk on the beaches, so bring repellent. The sea is warm, the beaches are lovely and the mountain scenery is dramatic, but be careful in the rain, when the road can be slippery and visibility poor.
t.pariquera abaixo state park@-24.6,-47.8:
Between the Ribeira de Iguape river and the coast of southern São Paulo state, the land is low, green and wet, covered in a patchwork of banana plantations, rice fields, mangroves and patches of dense Atlantic Forest. The Pariquera-Abaixo State Park protects one of these patches, part of the larger network of Atlantic Forest reserves of southeast Brazil listed by UNESCO in 1999, a region that holds some of the most extensive surviving stretches of this once vast forest.

The Vale do Ribeira, as the region is known, is one of the least developed corners of São Paulo state, and that has helped preserve its nature. The forest is home to a huge diversity of plants and animals, from bromeliads and orchids to toucans, monkeys and, deeper in the hills, the elusive jaguar. Rivers wind slowly through the lowlands, and in the morning, mist rises from the water and the forest echoes with birdsong. The town of Registro, nearby, was a centre of Japanese immigration in the early twentieth century, and its tea plantations and Japanese heritage are still visible today.

The main artery is the BR-116, the Régis Bittencourt highway, linking São Paulo with Curitiba, busy with trucks and known for its heavy traffic. Side roads to the coast and into the hills are quieter, winding through banana groves and small towns, though surfaces vary and rain can turn unpaved roads to mud. The climate is warm and humid all year, with heavy rains in summer, from December to March, when storms can be sudden and intense.

Fuel is available in Pariquera-Açu, Registro and Iguape, as well as along the highway. Iguape, founded in the sixteenth century, is one of the oldest towns in Brazil, with a colonial centre and a pilgrimage church that attracts thousands. Try local dishes based on fish and shrimp, banana sweets and cakes, and fresh tropical fruit from roadside stalls. Bring insect repellent and rain gear, and allow time for a walk in the forest, where the variety of greens is extraordinary.
t.sairam ugam state national nature park i:
In the far south of Kazakhstan, east of the city of Shymkent, the Western Tien Shan mountains rise abruptly from the steppe in a wall of snow-capped peaks, deep gorges and forests of juniper, walnut and wild fruit trees. The Sairam-Ugam National Park protects a large part of these mountains, and it is one of the components of the Western Tien Shan World Heritage site, listed by UNESCO in 2016 together with areas in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan.

The mountains are a biodiversity hotspot, home to many species of plants found nowhere else, including wild tulips, the ancestors of many garden varieties, which bloom in spring across the slopes. Wild apples, apricots and walnuts grow in the forests, and the park is home to snow leopards, ibex, bears and golden eagles. The valleys are watered by rivers fed by melting snow, and in spring and early summer, the meadows are a riot of colour. Traditional herding still takes place in the mountains, with yurts and livestock dotting the high pastures in summer.

Riding in this area means a mix of good roads and rough tracks. The main road from Shymkent to Taraz and on to Almaty is generally in decent condition, with long straight stretches across the steppe, while roads into the mountains, towards the villages of Tyulkubas and Kokterek and the park entrance, can be narrow, steep and unpaved. Traffic is light in the mountains, but livestock and potholes are common. Weather can change quickly, with snow possible at higher elevations in spring and autumn, and summer heat on the plains.

Tyulkubas, a town of around ten thousand, has fuel, shops and basic services, while Shymkent, a city of over a million people, has everything you need. Pumps are not hard to find, though it is worth choosing the busier, branded ones. Kazakh cuisine is meat-heavy: try beshbarmak, boiled meat with noodles, and shashlik, grilled meat on skewers, as well as kumis, fermented mare's milk, if you are adventurous. Permits may be required for some parts of the park, so check in advance.
t.sairam ugam state national nature park s:
The Western Tien Shan comes down to meet the steppe here, in the far south of Kazakhstan, and the Sairam-Ugam National Park protects a big piece of that collision. Snowy ridges rise above deep valleys with rushing rivers, forests of juniper, birch and wild fruit trees, and high meadows full of flowers in early summer. The park is part of the Western Tien Shan World Heritage Site, shared with Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan and listed in 2016, a region known as one of the places where many fruit trees, including wild apples, walnuts and apricots, have their origins. The wildlife includes snow leopards, ibex, bears and the endemic Menzbier's marmot.

In spring, the slopes bloom with tulips, including the large red Greig's tulip, a wild ancestor of many garden varieties, and the meadows are a riot of colour. Shepherds bring their flocks up to the high pastures in summer, living in yurts and selling kumis, fermented mare's milk, to passing visitors. The neighbouring Aksu-Zhabagly reserve, founded in 1926, is the oldest nature reserve in Central Asia.

Riding into the park means leaving the main roads behind. The asphalt roads from Shymkent and Lenger lead to the foothills, but beyond them, the routes into the valleys are mostly gravel or dirt, with river crossings, steep climbs and rough sections. A dual sport or adventure bike is the right tool, along with good tyres, spare parts and the skills to deal with whatever the mountains throw at you. Permits are needed to enter the national park, and some areas near the borders are restricted, so check the rules in advance and register with the park authorities.

Lenger, about thirty kilometres away, is a small town with fuel and shops, and Shymkent, one of the largest cities in Kazakhstan, has everything you could need. Fuel is cheap, but stations are spaced far apart in rural areas, so carry extra. The weather in the mountains can be unpredictable, with hot days, cold nights and sudden storms, and snow can block the high valleys from autumn to spring. The best time to visit is from May to September, and the food in the villages is simple and filling: plov, shashlik, laghman noodles and bread straight from the tandoor oven.
t.site of ornek@42.9,72.1:
Ornek is a place where the Silk Road becomes tangible in the grass. It lies in the foothills of the Talas Alatau, at the western end of the Tian Shan, in southern Kazakhstan near the border with Kyrgyzstan, and it was a settlement of the Turkic peoples who dominated these steppes between roughly the eighth and twelfth centuries. Its earthen walls, the outline of its citadel and the lines of houses are visible as low mounds, and scattered around are balbals, carved stone figures with faces, raised by the Turks to honour the dead. Ornek, like nearby Kulan and Kostobe, was inscribed as part of the Silk Roads corridor running from Chang'an to the Tian Shan.

The landscape is the thing. Behind the site the mountains rise steeply, snow-capped for much of the year, and in front the land rolls away in wave after wave of grassland towards the Chu and Talas valleys. In spring the steppe is green and splashed with poppies and tulips, which grow wild here; by late summer it turns gold and dry. Horses and sheep graze freely, and you may see shepherds on horseback, a scene that has not changed much since the Silk Road caravans passed through.

Riding here means good tarmac in the valley and rough tracks everywhere else. The highway between Taraz and Bishkek runs along the valley floor, and from it gravel roads lead up into the foothills; the final approach may be little more than a dirt track. Distances are long, villages are small and services are sparse, so a dual-sport bike and some self-reliance make sense. Weather changes fast near the mountains, with afternoon storms in summer and cold nights at any time of year.

There are no towns of any size immediately nearby; Taraz, the regional capital, is the nearest city with reliable fuel, shops and accommodation, and smaller villages along the main road have basic shops and occasionally a fuel station. Carry extra fuel and water if you plan to explore. Local hospitality is generous; you may be invited for tea, bread and kumys, fermented mare's milk, which is an acquired taste but an important part of steppe culture.
t.chauas ecological station@-24.7,-47.7:
The south coast of São Paulo state is a world away from the megacity a few hours to the north. Here, around the old town of Iguape, the Ribeira de Iguape river reaches the sea through a maze of channels, mangroves, islands and lagoons, backed by the forested slopes of the Serra do Mar. The Chauás Ecological Station protects a piece of lowland Atlantic Forest and restinga, the sandy coastal vegetation, near Iguape, and it is part of the Atlantic Forest Southeast Reserves, listed by UNESCO in 1999. The Atlantic Forest once covered much of the Brazilian coast; today only a fraction remains, and this region holds some of the largest continuous stretches.

Wildlife is abundant, though often hidden. The red-tailed parrot, endemic to this stretch of coast, nests on islands and in the forest, and herons, egrets, spoonbills and scarlet ibises feed in the mangroves. Dolphins swim in the estuary, and the forest is home to monkeys, sloths and a variety of reptiles. The station itself is mainly for research and conservation rather than tourism.

Iguape is one of the oldest towns in Brazil, founded in the sixteenth century, and its colonial centre, with whitewashed houses and the basilica of Bom Jesus de Iguape, is a pleasant place to walk. Every August, pilgrims come in huge numbers for the festival of Bom Jesus. In the nineteenth century, a canal called the Valo Grande was dug to link the river with the port, but it eroded and widened dramatically, diverting much of the river's flow and silting up the port, a cautionary tale of engineering gone wrong.

The roads here are quiet, mostly paved but sometimes potholed, running through banana plantations, forest and small villages. From Iguape a bridge leads to Ilha Comprida, a long barrier island with wide sandy beaches. The main road from the BR-116, the highway between São Paulo and Curitiba, passes through Pariquera-Açu and Jacupiranga before reaching the coast. Iguape, a town of some twenty-four thousand, can refuel you and feed you, with places serving fresh fish and seafood, including the local manjuba, a small fish fried crisp. The climate is warm and humid year round, with heavy summer rain, so expect wet roads and pack accordingly.
t.site of akyrtas@43.0,71.8:
Out on the steppe east of Taraz, in southern Kazakhstan, the remains of Akyrtas are a puzzle that no one has fully solved. Rows of massive blocks of red sandstone lie in a vast rectangle, the foundations of a palace or fortified complex that seems to have been planned on an enormous scale and never finished. Its date is usually placed around the eighth or ninth century, but who built it, an Arab governor, a Turkic ruler of the Karluks, or someone else entirely, remains open. The stones are carefully cut, the layout is formal, with a central courtyard and rooms around it, and the whole thing sits in an empty landscape that only deepens the mystery. It is part of the transnational World Heritage site of the Silk Roads.

This was the Talas valley, one of the great corridors of the Silk Road between China and the West. Not far away, in 751, Arab and Chinese armies met in the Battle of Talas, a clash that marked the limit of Tang Chinese power in Central Asia. Taraz, under its old name of Talas, was a major trading city for centuries, and the mausoleums of Aisha Bibi and Babaji Khatun near the city are among the most beautiful early Islamic buildings in Central Asia, decorated with terracotta tiles.

The landscape is wide and open. To the south the Kyrgyz Ala-Too range rises like a wall, snow-capped for much of the year, and the plain in front is covered in grass and wildflowers in spring, burnt gold by late summer. The wind blows across the steppe almost constantly, and the light is clear and hard. Herds of horses and sheep graze freely, and you may see eagles circling overhead.

The main road from Taraz to Almaty passes not far from the site, a long, straight highway in variable condition, with heavy trucks and some brave overtaking. The last stretch to Akyrtas is a minor road or track that can be rough and dusty. There are no facilities at the site. Taraz, a city of several hundred thousand people, has fuel, hotels and markets, and Sarykemer is the nearest town with basic services. Try the local food: beshbarmak, boiled meat with flat noodles, and kumys, fermented mare's milk, if you dare.
t.aksu jabagly state nature reserve main p:
Kazakhstan's oldest nature reserve sits where the western end of the Tien Shan meets the steppe, in the Talas Alatau range, and it was set aside as early as 1926. Aksu-Jabagly is a country of steep limestone gorges, high meadows and snowy ridges that climb above three thousand metres, and it forms part of the UNESCO listing for the Western Tien-Shan. The Aksu canyon cuts through the heart of it, with walls hung with juniper, and on some rock faces you can find petroglyphs left by herders and hunters thousands of years ago.

The reserve is best known for its tulips. The wild species that grew on these slopes, including Greig's tulip and Kaufmann's tulip, are the ancestors of many garden varieties, and in April and May the foothills turn red, yellow and orange. Botanists also point out that the nearby mountains are the original home of the wild apple, which gives the whole region a deep biological interest. Among the animals are brown bears, lynx, argali sheep, ibex and, high up and very rarely seen, snow leopards.

This is not casual riding country. Access to the reserve is controlled, and you need permission and, usually, a ranger or guide to enter the core area; the tracks beyond the village of Zhabagly are rough gravel, fording streams and climbing steeply. The tarmac to the village itself is straightforward, through steppe villages with orchards and the shimmering line of mountains to the south. Spring is the best time, when the tulips are out and the weather is mild, though it can still be cold and wet at altitude; summer is hot on the plains and cool in the hills, and winter brings deep snow.

Zhabagly, a village of about two thousand people, has a few shops and is the nearest base, but fuel is better sought in the larger towns of the district, Turar Ryskulov and Tyulkubas, the latter being the bigger of the two. Shymkent, the big city of the south, is the place to stock up before a longer trip. Local hospitality in the villages is warm, with tea, bread, dried fruit and a lot of questions. If you stay overnight, ask about the guest houses near the reserve gate, which often serve a simple dinner of lamb and noodles.
t.site of kostobe@43.0,71.5:
The ruined town of Kostobe lies in the broad valley of the Talas river, a few kilometres from Sarykemer and about sixteen from Taraz, in the south of Kazakhstan. It belongs to the string of settlements along the Silk Road that UNESCO recognised in 2014 as the Chang'an-Tianshan corridor, and its low mounds and eroded walls recall a time when caravans passed through here between China, Central Asia and the Middle East. Details of the excavations are the business of archaeologists, but the general picture is clear: a walled medieval trading town on fertile land, close to a river and a major route.

The region is famous for one event above all. In 751, near the Talas river, an army of the Abbasid caliphate met a Tang Chinese force, and the Chinese were defeated. The battle is often said to mark the end of Tang expansion westward and, according to a well-known tradition, to have passed papermaking technology from Chinese prisoners to the Islamic world, though historians debate the details. Taraz, the nearby city, is one of the oldest in Kazakhstan, and it keeps older treasures: the Aisha Bibi mausoleum, a little way west of the city, is a small masterpiece of eleventh or twelfth century terracotta tilework.

The riding is easy and open. The main road between Almaty, Taraz and Shymkent crosses a plain with the snowy line of the Alatau always to the south, and the surface is mostly good, with heavy trucks and some stretches of rough patching. Spring brings green fields and poppies, summer is very hot, and autumn is a lovely time of golden light and fruit stalls at the roadside. Winter is cold, with ice and strong winds. Sarykemer is a small town of about fifteen thousand, and has fuel, shops and cafes; Taraz, a city of more than three hundred and fifty thousand, has everything.

Ruins like this have little for the casual visitor to see, since time and ploughing have worn them down, so go with a modest expectation and an interest in the landscape. Stand on a mound, look at the mountains, and think of how many travellers have stopped at that very place. In Taraz, a bowl of beshbarmak, boiled meat with flat noodles, is the traditional meal for guests, and the tea is always strong.
t.ubatuba@-23.4,-45.1:
Ubatuba has more than eighty beaches, and surfers say the exact number depends on how much you walk. The name is from the Tupi language and is often said to mean place of canoe-trees, referring to the big trees the Tupinambá carved into boats. Beyond the beaches, the town sits between the sea and the Serra do Mar, a steep mountain wall covered in Atlantic forest, one of the richest and most threatened ecosystems in Brazil. The result is a coast where you can swim in the morning, walk to a waterfall in the afternoon and see toucans at dusk.

In the sixteenth century this was Tupinambá territory, and the Confederation of the Tamoios, an alliance of Tupinambá chiefs who fought against the Portuguese, was based here. The old centre has a small colonial church and a handful of low houses by the harbour, but the town is mainly a laid-back holiday place, with surf shops, pousadas and open-air restaurants. Fishing boats still unload on the quay in the morning, and the fish market is a lively place to buy shrimp and squid.

The riding is excellent. The Rio-Santos highway, BR-101, passes through Ubatuba, rolling over headlands and descending to beaches in a ribbon of curves, with views of islands, and the surface is generally good. Another favourite is the Oswaldo Cruz road, SP-125, which climbs the Serra do Mar from the coast toward Taubaté with dozens of bends, forest, mist and tight hairpins. Mist and rain can make the mountain stretch slippery, so check conditions and avoid it after dark. The summer holiday period and carnival bring heavy traffic on the coast road.

Ubatuba is a town of nearly eighty thousand and offers fuel stations, workshops, supermarkets and every kind of restaurant. Try a moqueca, the fish stew with coconut milk, or a grilled fish with banana. Secure parking is easy at most pousadas. Insect repellent is a good idea in the evenings, and sunscreen is essential at the beaches. The best weather is from April to October, when the humidity eases, though the sea is warmer in summer.
t.site of kulan@42.9,72.7:
Nobody lives at Kulan now, except sheep and the odd herder, but in the early Middle Ages it was a town of the Silk Road, a stop on the route that ran from China across the Tian Shan foothills into Central Asia. The plain it stands on lies in the south of Kazakhstan, in the Zhambyl region, between the snowy ridges of the Kyrgyz Alatau, which rise to the south, and the dry steppe stretching north to Lake Balkhash and beyond. Here the Chu river valley and the Taraz road made a natural highway for caravans, and the settlement of Kulan, in the early medieval centuries, was a market and a staging post, with the mud-brick walls, towers and a citadel typical of the region. It was listed in 2014, together with Kostobe and many other sites, as part of the Silk Roads network's Tian-Shan corridor.

Little remains above ground, and what is left reads best as bumps and ridges in the grass, with a few eroded walls. The wind, the larks and the huge sky do most of the work for you. Archaeologists have found pottery and coins that tell of trade with Sogdian merchants, who carried silk, glass, and ideas, and of Turkic peoples who ruled the steppe.

For a rider, the road is part of the point. Roads in southern Kazakhstan are mostly good along the main routes, and the long, straight stretches across the steppe require attention against fatigue and strong crosswinds. Summers are hot and dry, with temperatures above thirty-five degrees, and winters bitterly cold, so spring and early autumn are the best seasons. Be careful of livestock on the road at dusk, and of loose gravel when the tarmac gives way to a side track.

Fuel can be found in Lugovoy, a town of over ten thousand people on the main route, and the city of Taraz, further west, has much more. Outside those towns, stations can be far apart, so top up when you can. Roadside cafes serve beshbarmak, boiled meat on noodles, and fresh bread with kumys, the fermented mare's milk, an acquired taste.

Take water and a hat, and a good sense of direction, because signs can be sparse.
t.sary chelek state biosphere nature reser:
Sary-Chelek means yellow bucket, and nobody quite agrees on why. The name belongs to a lake in the Chatkal range of south-western Kyrgyzstan, a deep, clear body of water at the bottom of a forested valley, which was formed when a landslide, probably set off by an earthquake, dammed the river long ago. The water takes on shades from emerald to deep blue depending on the light and the season, and the shore is fringed with spruce, with walnut and apple woods on the lower slopes, and meadows full of flowers in June. It lies at about 1,900 metres above the sea, and the cold clean air has a scent of pine.

The lake is the centre of the Sary-Chelek State Biosphere Reserve, set up in 1959 and recognised by UNESCO in 1978, and it protects an area of forest and mountain that holds seven lakes in all, with bears, wolves, lynx, Siberian ibex and a long list of birds. The walnut forests of southern Kyrgyzstan, which are among the largest wild walnut woods in the world, are the other great treasure of this region, and the whole area is a biodiversity hotspot. The reserve requires a permit and an entry fee, which you can usually arrange at the entrance or through a local guide.

Reaching the lake is half the adventure. The roads from the lowlands of the Fergana valley climb through hill villages and orchards into the mountains, with sections of tarmac, long stretches of gravel and the occasional river crossing, and a bike with good ground clearance and some off-road capability is the right tool. After rain, the surface can turn to slippery mud, and landslides sometimes cut the way. Distances are longer than they look, and the light fades early in the valleys. Do not plan on riding at night.

Homestays near the entrance offer beds, hot food and tea, and the family will often serve fresh bread with cream and jam, and mutton soup. The best season is from late May to September, with the autumn colours in October. Take warm clothing and rain gear, because the mountain weather changes quickly, and bring cash in small notes, as cards are rarely accepted.
t.bishkek@42.9,74.6:
Bishkek lies at the foot of the Kyrgyz Ala-Too, the northern range of the Tian Shan, and on a clear morning the snow peaks seem close enough to touch from the city's long boulevards. The capital of Kyrgyzstan was a small fort and trading post in the nineteenth century, and was then rebuilt as a Soviet city named Frunze, after the Bolshevik commander born nearby. The legacy is a grid of broad, straight streets lined with poplars and elms, Soviet apartment blocks, wide squares, and statues, including the one of Manas, the hero of the national epic, who stands in front of the main square, Ala-Too.

For riders, Bishkek is the logical start of the Issyk-Kul loop. The city has about nine hundred thousand people, and it has everything: fuel on every main road, supermarkets, bike shops and mechanics of variable quality, and a wide choice of guesthouses. Traffic is dense, with minibuses called marshrutkas stopping without warning, and the driving style is assertive, so keep your wits about you. Pavements and drains can be uneven, and potholes can be severe on the edge of the city.

The Osh Bazaar is a good place to spend a morning, a noisy market of bread, dried fruit, nuts, spices, meat and everything else, and the food stalls offer plov, laghman noodles, samsa pastries and manty dumplings. A bowl of beshbarmak, boiled meat with noodles, is the national dish, and kumis, fermented mare's milk, is an acquired taste to be tried at least once. To the south, the Ala Archa National Park lies about forty kilometres away, a mountain valley with glaciers and alpine meadows, easily reached by a road that climbs steadily.

Heading east, the road to Lake Issyk-Kul passes through the Chuy valley, past the Burana Tower, an old minaret left from the medieval city of Balasagun, and then through the Boom Gorge, a narrow, dramatic canyon beside the Chu river. The road is usually in fair shape but wind, trucks and roadworks can make it testing.

The best months for riding are from May to September, with heat in July and August and possible snow on the passes in spring and autumn. Carry cash in the local currency, the som.
t.campos do jordao@-22.7,-45.6:
Campos do Jordão is the highest town in Brazil, at 1,628 metres in the Serra da Mantiqueira, and it behaves like it. The air is cool, even on summer evenings, pine and araucaria trees line the streets, and in winter the temperature can fall close to freezing, which draws visitors from São Paulo who want to wear a scarf and eat fondue. The architecture leans toward Swiss and Bavarian chalets, a style that began when the town became a health resort in the early twentieth century, prized for its clean, dry mountain air as a place to recover from tuberculosis.

The town spreads along a valley, with the lively Capivari district at its centre, full of chocolate shops, restaurants and boutiques, and quieter quarters up the hillsides. Each July, the Winter Festival of classical music, held since 1970, brings orchestras and soloists to concert halls and open-air stages, and the town fills with visitors. The Horto Florestal, a forest reserve on the edge of town, shelters araucarias, streams and trails, while a chairlift climbs to the Morro do Elefante for a view over the valley.

The road up from the lowlands is a pleasure for riders, with long, curving ascents through eucalyptus and pine, cooler air at every bend and good views. The tarmac is mostly smooth, though weekends see heavy traffic, particularly in July and on holidays, with lines of cars on the final approach. Fog and drizzle can arrive suddenly and the temperature drops quickly, so a warm layer helps. Mornings are best, with fresh air and light traffic, and mid-week is far calmer.

Fuel is available in the town, and the whole area is well supplied with restaurants, bakeries and cafés. Local specialities include trout, pinhão, fondue and hot chocolate, and prices rise in high season. Parking in the centre is tight and fills quickly, so choose a hotel with secure parking if you stay. The streets are steep and can be slippery in the wet, so ride carefully.
t.mogi das cruzes@-23.5,-46.2:
Mogi das Cruzes is a big city on the eastern fringe of São Paulo, with more than three hundred thousand people, and for a rider heading toward the Serra do Mar and the coast it is the practical last stop before the road gets serious. It sits on the Tietê river valley in a landscape of low hills and market gardens, with the mountains of the Serra do Mar forming a dark wall to the south. The city has a large community of Japanese descent, who settled in the area in the early twentieth century and made it a centre of vegetable and flower growing, and you will see their mark in the markets, restaurants and festivals.

The city's main festival is the Festa do Divino, a religious celebration with processions, music and food that has taken place for generations. The old centre has a cathedral, small squares and shops, and the surroundings include parks of Atlantic forest that survive in patches between the farms and suburbs. The air is warm and humid, and in summer afternoon thunderstorms are common, with heavy rain that can make the roads slick in minutes.

As a fuel stop, Mogi is simple. The city has many stations along the main roads, open for long hours, and prices are in line with the São Paulo region. The traffic around the city can be heavy, especially at rush hours and on weekends, with lorries, buses and cars sharing the highways. If you are heading for the coast, an early start helps you beat the worst of it. Take care at junctions and on the multi-lane roads, where drivers can be aggressive and lane discipline is loose.

Food is cheap and good. Small restaurants serve the Brazilian plate of rice, beans, meat and salad, and the Japanese influence gives you the chance to try sushi, noodle dishes or a pastel, a fried pastry filled with cheese or meat, bought from a market stall. Coffee is strong and sweet, and a pão de queijo, cheese bread, is a good snack for the road.

Beyond the city, the road begins to climb toward the Serra do Mar and the coast, with forest closing in and the temperature dropping. Check your tyres and lights, carry a rain jacket and fill the tank fully, because the mountain sections have fewer stations. Brazil drives on the right, and local riders are quick, so keep a safe distance and stay alert.
t.serra do mar road@-23.4,-45.9:
The Serra do Mar is the great escarpment that runs along the coast of south-eastern Brazil, a wall of forested mountains between the São Paulo plateau and the Atlantic, and crossing it is one of the main events of any ride from the city to the sea. The roads that climb or descend it, such as the Rodovia dos Tamoios, thread through dense Atlantic forest, one of the most diverse and most threatened ecosystems on earth. The trees are tall and wrapped in vines, bromeliads and ferns, and the air is thick with the smell of wet leaves and soil.

The area near Santa Branca and Jacareí lies in the Paraíba valley, on the plateau side of the range, where reservoirs and farmland fill the broad floor of the valley. From here the roads lead up and over the mountains toward the coast, and the change in scenery is rapid. On the plateau, the air is drier and cooler, with pasture and eucalyptus, and as the road rises into the forest, the temperature drops and cloud begins to gather. At the crest, the mist can be so thick that visibility falls to a few metres, and the road emerges below it into sunshine or a downpour.

The ride is demanding in the best way. The bends are tight and often blind, the surface can be wet and slick with moss and mud, and heavy trucks use the same lanes, so overtaking needs judgement. Wet weather is common, with sudden downpours, and fog is frequent in the mornings. Care is required on descents, where brakes can overheat and the road drops steeply, and the locals know that a clear day can turn into a grey one in minutes. Landslides sometimes close sections after heavy rain, so check the conditions.

Santa Branca, about two kilometres away, is a small town with basic services, and Jacareí, a city of over two hundred thousand, lies about eleven kilometres off, with plenty of fuel, food and repairs. There are few stations on the mountain, so fill the tank before the climb. Roadside stalls and small restaurants appear at viewpoints and sell snacks and fruit.

The wildlife in the forest is rich, with toucans, monkeys and many butterflies, though you will seldom see them from a bike. Stop at a viewpoint, if the clouds permit, and listen to the forest. It is a green, loud world.
t.ubatuba coast@-23.4,-45.1:

t.tremembe@-23.0,-45.5:
Tremembé lies in the flat green floor of the Paraíba valley, at just under six hundred metres, between two larger cities, Taubaté and Pindamonhangaba. It is not a place most riders choose to see for its own sake, but it is the foot of the mountain, and in a ride like this one, that makes it important. The town takes its name from the Tremembé people, who lived in this stretch of the valley long before the Portuguese reached it. Tremembé today has a population of about thirty thousand, a lively old centre with a square and a church, and the slightly confusing reputation of having a well-known prison on its outskirts. t.maria da fe@-22.3,-45.4:
At twelve hundred and seventy metres, Maria da Fé is one of the coldest towns in Minas Gerais, and the locals are proud of it. The ridge road here is what a rider hopes for in Brazil. The altitude keeps the air crisp, the surface is generally better than the lowland roads, and the bends are open and flowing, climbing through pasture, eucalyptus and small groves of pine. Traffic is light apart from the occasional truck and a lot of locals on small motorbikes. In winter the mornings can be cold enough for frost on the tarmac in shaded corners, and fog sits in the hollows until mid-morning, so wait until the sun reaches the road before you push on.

Evenings are cold, even in summer, so keep something warm in the bag. The best months for riding are May to September, when the air is dry, the skies are clear and the Mantiqueira shows its full outline on the horizon.
t.site of aktobe@43.2,74.0:
The Site of Aktobe is better known to archaeologists as Ak-Beshim, a ruined Silk Road town in the Chuy Valley of northern Kyrgyzstan, and it was once the city of Suyab. Around the seventh and eighth centuries it was a major stop for merchants, a Sogdian trading settlement and later a Turkic and Chinese Tang garrison town. Excavators found a Buddhist temple and also a Nestorian Christian church, a sign of how many faiths mingled on the road. The poet Li Bai, one of China's most famous, is said by some accounts to have been born here, though the matter is debated. Today it is a field of earthen mounds and low walls under open sky, and you need a bit of imagination to see the town.

The Chuy Valley is a broad, flat basin, hemmed in by the Kyrgyz Ala-Too range to the south, with the snow peaks standing clear above the plain on a bright day. The ground is good farmland, and the roads between villages are lined with poplars and irrigation ditches. From Bishkek, about sixty kilometres to the west, the highway to Tokmok is smooth and busy, with lorries and shared taxis. Beyond it, minor roads run off toward ruins and small villages, with patches of broken tarmac, gravel and the occasional cow.

Climb its tower for a view across the plain, and look at the collection of old stone figures called balbals nearby. Practical matters are simple. Tokmok has fuel, shops and small cafes with plov, lagman and fresh bread, and Bishkek has everything else. Summer is hot and dry, and the best months are May, June, September and early October. Do not expect shade at the site, and carry water. Dust follows any vehicle on side roads, and it is wise to keep a good distance from trucks.
t.santos@-24.0,-46.3:
Santos is Brazil's great port, the largest in Latin America, and for a rider who has spent the day on the coast road from Paraty, arriving feels like landing in a different century. The city sits on São Vicente island, across a channel from the mainland, and the harbour is crowded with cranes, container stacks and ships waiting for berths. Nearly everything Brazil sells to the world, coffee above all, passed through here at some point, and the old coffee exchange building, now a museum, still has its stained-glass ceiling and a tasting room.

Nearby São Vicente, a few kilometres away, claims to be the oldest town in Brazil, founded in 1532.

A rider should take care in heavy rain, when the surface turns slick, and on weekends and holidays, when the traffic is dense.

Late afternoon sun over the bay gives the whole harbour a golden light, and it is a fine way to finish a long ride.
t.sao roque de minas@-20.2,-46.4:
Sao Roque de Minas is a small town in the highlands of Minas Gerais, at the gateway to the Serra da Canastra National Park, a high plateau of grassland, rocky ridges and waterfalls that is the source of the Sao Francisco River, one of the longest rivers in Brazil. The gravel roads inside the park are rough, with loose stones, ruts and steep sections, and they become slippery after rain, so adventure bikes and a cautious pace are wise. The dry season, roughly May to September, is the best time to ride, with clear skies and cool mornings, while the summer months bring heavy afternoon storms. Mornings are crisp, and the light on the grassland is golden.

Queijo Canastra, a firm, tangy cow's-milk cheese made by hand on small farms and aged in the open air, is protected as a cultural heritage of Brazil, and you will find it for sale in roadside shops and in the town. Producers still use methods handed down over generations, and a visit to a farm, if you can arrange one, is memorable. Local cooking is hearty, with beans, pork, cornbread and fresh coffee, and a slice of cheese with a cup of coffee makes a fine stop.

Nature is the main draw. The park protects a large stretch of cerrado, the tropical savanna of central Brazil, a landscape of tall grass, twisted trees and rocky outcrops, and its wildlife includes the giant anteater, maned wolf, rhea and many birds. The Casca d'Anta waterfall, one of the highest in the region, drops over a cliff near the source of the Sao Francisco, and the spring itself is a small, quiet place where the great river begins.
