Fill up in a larger town before arriving, carry water, and check the weather before riding gravel. Respect the park rules and watch for wildlife on the road, especially at dusk.
t.suusamyr@42.2,74.0:
Suusamyr is a high, wide, windy valley in the heart of Kyrgyzstan, a long green bowl at more than two thousand metres between the Suusamyr-Too and Kyrgyz ranges, and in summer it is one of the best places in Central Asia to see a pastoral way of life that has hardly changed in centuries. There is no real town at the pin, only a scattering of villages, herders' yurts and the road, and the nearest settlement of any size is a long way off. The valley is famous for being cold: snow can fall in any month, and winter temperatures drop far below freezing.

The riding is exceptional. The road from Bishkek climbs to the Too-Ashuu Pass, at around 3,500 metres, passing through a long tunnel built in the 1950s before descending to the valley floor, where the tarmac runs flat and straight for dozens of kilometres between rolling hills. Further on, the road to Talas climbs over the Ala-Bel pass, with fresh tarmac in places and rough patches elsewhere, and enormous views. The surface can be broken by frost, with potholes and washouts after rain, and livestock regularly wander across. Altitude affects both rider and engine, so go slowly, carry warm layers and drink plenty of water. The riding season is short, from June to September, and weather can swing from hot sun to hail in an hour.

The valley is a jailoo, a summer pasture, and from June to September herding families arrive from the lowlands with their horses, sheep and cattle, setting up felt yurts on the green slopes. The people are Kyrgyz, descendants of nomadic tribes who have herded here for centuries, and hospitality is a matter of pride. A rider who stops near a yurt may be invited for tea, bread and cream, and a bowl of kymyz, fermented mare's milk, which has a sour, fizzy tang. The Soviet era brought collective farms and roads, and the remains of those times can still be seen in some villages.

Nature is vast and clean. The valley floor is covered in grass and wildflowers, with snow-capped peaks along the horizon, and eagles, hawks and marmots are common. The air smells of grass, dung smoke and cold water, and the night sky is amazing. Rivers run clear and cold from the glaciers, and horses graze on the slopes.

Fill the tank in Bishkek or before the pass, since fuel is limited in the valley, and carry extra if you can. Bring cold-weather gear, food, water and a spare tube, and tell someone your plans, since mobile coverage drops out.
t.monte verde@-22.9,-46.0:
Pine trees, wooden chalets and a fondue on the menu: this corner of Minas Gerais does a convincing impression of the Alps. Monte Verde is a small village at about 1,500 metres in the Serra da Mantiqueira, near the border between Minas Gerais and São Paulo, and it has built a whole identity on being cold. Winter nights drop close to freezing, the buildings are styled with steep roofs and timber, and visitors flock from São Paulo for open fires, chocolate and a feeling of being somewhere else.

The ride from Campos do Jordão, which at around 1,600 metres is among the highest cities in Brazil, passes through the Mantiqueira's upland landscape of pine and eucalyptus forest, farmland and rocky ridges. The roads are winding, with climbs, drops and hairpins, and the surface quality can be uneven, with potholes after rain, so take care. Fog often settles in the valleys in the morning, and in summer afternoon thunderstorms are common, so set off early and keep a rain jacket handy. The last approach to the village is steep and narrow.

Above the village, the Pedra Redonda and the Chapéu do Bispo give views over ranges of blue ridges, and forest trails lead to waterfalls and streams. Birdwatchers look for the Atlantic forest species, such as toucans and tanagers, and the air has the resinous smell of pine. The village streets are small, lined with shops selling jams, cheese, wool and chocolate, and restaurants that serve fondue, trout and hearty stews.

Monte Verde has a few fuel options, but supplies are limited and weekends get crowded, so the safer bet is to fill the tank in Camanducaia, sixteen kilometres away with nearly eighteen thousand people, and Joanópolis, a bit further. Book accommodation in advance for winter weekends and holidays, when the village fills up and prices rise. Bring warm clothing at any time of year, as evenings are chilly, and take extra care in the streets after dark, when they are steep, wet and poorly lit.
t.capitolio@-20.6,-46.0:
Capitólio owes its fame to a lake that was built by accident, in a sense. In the 1960s the Furnas dam flooded the valley of the Rio Grande in south-west Minas Gerais, and the water rose up between the old canyons, leaving a huge reservoir with sheer rock walls, small islands and hidden coves. Today it is Brazil's inland playground, and the small town of Capitólio on its shore is the base for boat trips that run along the canyon, past waterfalls pouring straight from the cliffs into green water.

On the water, take the safety rules seriously. The cliffs are tall and rockfalls have caused accidents there, so boats must keep the distances set by the operators and authorities, and it is sensible to choose a licensed company and follow the crew's instructions. The water is calm and clear, and in the quiet parts, you can swim or paddle in sheltered coves. Early morning is best, before the crowds and the wind.

The ride is gentle and pleasant, a mix of rolling farmland, coffee plantations, pasture and low hills, with roads that wind between fields and small towns, with enough bends to keep things interesting. It forms part of a loop that also takes in the Serra da Canastra, a high plateau of grassland and waterfalls where the São Francisco river begins its long journey to the Atlantic. The weather is warm for most of the year, with heavy storms in the summer afternoons, so start early, and watch for animals and slow farm vehicles.

Minas Gerais has a deserved reputation for food, and cheese from the Canastra region is among the best, as are the cakes, sweet fruit pastes and strong coffee. Restaurants by the lake serve fresh river fish with farofa, and the town has plenty of pousadas. Capitólio is small and gets crowded on weekends and holidays, so book ahead and arrive early, and fill the tank at a larger town such as Piuí, about nineteen kilometres away, if there is any doubt about supplies. Bring sun protection and a swimsuit.
t.ala archa@42.6,74.5:
Within an hour's ride of Bishkek's traffic and concrete you can be standing in a glacial valley with a peak above you and a cold stream beside your boots. Ala Archa is a national park in the Kyrgyz Ala-Too, the northern range of the Tian Shan, and it is the capital's favourite weekend escape. The name is usually taken to mean something like the variegated juniper, after the Tian Shan junipers that cling to the slopes. The valley rises from the foothills toward a cluster of glaciers and snowy summits above four thousand metres.

The road from the city is tarmac nearly all the way, running south across the plain toward the mountains, past the village at the mouth of the gorge, and into the park, where a modest fee is charged at the gate. Bends are gentle, the road narrows and rises through spruce and juniper, and then the valley opens out into meadows with the river braiding through boulders. Beyond a certain point the track becomes rough, so most riders park and walk. Traffic builds on weekends, with picnickers, school groups and trekkers, so a weekday morning is much calmer.

What you are looking at is classic alpine Asia. Ridges of grey rock, streaks of snow, and a little further up, the Ak-Sai glacier and a climbers' hut higher still. Marmots whistle from the scree, ibex and snow leopards live higher up but you will be extraordinarily lucky to see either, and golden eagles ride the thermals. The air smells of juniper, wet stone and, near the cafe, grilled shashlik. Weather swings quickly: sunshine can turn into hail within an hour, so pack a waterproof.

For practicalities, remember that this is a small outpost, not a town. Fuel is a matter for Bishkek, a good half hour back, so leave with a full tank. There are a few basic guesthouses and cafes near the park entrance and a small place to buy water and snacks. In summer you can walk to the Ak-Sai waterfall in a few hours, and in the shoulder seasons the valley is quiet and lovely. For a first taste of Kyrgyz mountains, it is hard to beat.
t.too ashuu pass@42.3,73.8:
Too Ashuu is the point on the main road south from Bishkek where the country changes character. North of the pass, the highway crosses the Chuy plain with its fields, towns and traffic. South of it, you drop into a high, empty world of grass, yurts and sheep, the Suusamyr valley, with the Ala-Too wall rolling on in every direction. The pass lies at about 3,500 metres on the Kyrgyz Ala-Too, and the road across it is the central artery of the north-south link that joins Bishkek to Osh, built in the Soviet period when nobody was counting the cost.

The road hauls itself up a narrow gorge, climbing through a flight of hairpins that clings to the valley side, with trucks grinding along ahead and a river thundering below. A tunnel, built in the 1950s and a little over two kilometres long, carries the road through the crest and is notorious for its poor lighting, fumes, wet surface and the way oncoming drivers use the middle. Take it slowly, keep your visor clear, and be prepared to be seen. On the far side the road emerges into daylight, the valley widens, and the air is thin and cold.

Weather here is a character in its own right. Snow can fall in any month, fog can close the gorge in minutes, and wind funnels through the tunnel portals. In winter avalanches and ice make the pass a serious proposition. The best riding window is mid-summer to early autumn, early in the day, when the trucks are fewer and the sky is clear. A jacket for the south side is not optional, even if it is hot in Bishkek.

Fuel is an important detail. There is little on the climb itself, so refill before you go, at Sosnovka or farther back on the plain, and again when you drop to the Suusamyr side. Small roadside cafes sell tea, bread and plov, and you will find stalls offering kymyz, fermented mare's milk, a drink that tastes much worse than it sounds good. Stop at the top for a photograph, check your tyre pressures and layers, then ride on: ahead lies one of Central Asia's best long days.
t.talas@42.5,72.2:
Talas sits in a valley of its own, in the far northwest of Kyrgyzstan, hemmed in by the Kyrgyz Ala-Too to the south and the border with Kazakhstan to the north. It is a town of about thirty-five thousand people, and a place that Kyrgyz people regard with special warmth because it is closely tied to Manas, the hero of the country's great oral epic. Said to be one of the longest poems in the world, the epic follows Manas and his companions as they unite the Kyrgyz tribes, and the Manas Ordo complex near town, with a mausoleum said to be the hero's tomb, draws visitors from across the country.

Talas also appears in a quite different story. In the year 751, an army of the Tang dynasty clashed here with forces of the Abbasid Caliphate, in a battle that marked the high-water line of Chinese power in Central Asia. Tradition holds that Chinese prisoners taken after the fight passed the secrets of papermaking westward. Historians argue over the details, but the legend suits the place, which has always been a crossroads of the Silk Road.

Getting here is a ride in itself. Coming from the Suusamyr valley, the road crosses the Ala-Bel pass, a little over three thousand metres, and descends toward the Talas plain through green slopes and then farmland. Bends are tidy, the surface is decent in places and rough in others, and livestock and trucks share the lane with you. The valley below is warm, irrigated and fertile, with orchards, poplars and fields of beans, quite unlike the high pastures above. Spring and early autumn are the pick: blossoms, or gold, and no heat.

As a town stop, Talas does everything well. It is large enough for fuel, shops, pharmacies, small hotels and plenty of cafes, and it is a sensible place to resupply before or after the mountains. Try the local manty dumplings or lagman noodles, drink plenty of tea, and enjoy the unhurried pace. There is a bazaar worth a wander, and the people, as in much of Kyrgyzstan, tend to be curious about a foreign rider and quick to offer a seat.
t.osh@40.5,72.8:
Osh claims to be around three thousand years old, and for once the claim does not feel absurd. The city sits at the eastern edge of the Fergana valley, where the flat, hot cotton country runs into the first folds of the Pamir-Alay, and it has been a stopping point on the Silk Road for as long as caravans have crossed this region. With about two hundred thousand people, it is Kyrgyzstan's second city and, in temperament, the southern capital: louder, hotter, more Uzbek-influenced and rather prouder than Bishkek.

The thing you cannot miss is Sulaiman-Too, a rocky ridge that rises abruptly from the middle of the city. For centuries it has been a place of pilgrimage, with caves, shrines and a tradition that Muslims and earlier believers considered it sacred. On top is a small stone house said to have been used by Babur, the Fergana prince who went on to found the Mughal dynasty in India. The mountain is on the UNESCO list, and the climb up its stone steps is short enough to do before breakfast, with views over rooftops and the distant mountains.

The Jayma bazaar, stretching along the Ak-Buura river, is the other essential. It is huge and noisy, a place to buy fruit, spices, bread, felt, knives, melons and anything else you can imagine. Eat samsa, the baked pastries, straight from the oven, and lagman or plov for lunch. Sellers will not mind if you wander for an hour without buying. This is also where the long Pamir Highway begins, running south through Sary-Tash to Tajikistan, so riders tend to arrive here with a to-do list and leave with stories.

The town is large enough that fuel, spare parts, banks, SIM cards, laundries and hotels are all easy to find, and that makes it an important reset point before the mountains. Traffic is busy and hot, with shared taxis weaving through, so ride defensively. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; July and August can be brutally hot on the plain. Fill your tank before heading south, because the high country has few reliable pumps.
t.aksu zhabagly@42.3,70.5:
Aksu-Zhabagly is Kazakhstan's oldest nature reserve, founded in 1926, and it sits where the Western Tian Shan meets the end of the Talas Alatau. The protected area covers a wide altitude range, from steppe foothills to glaciers, and the result is a startling variety of habitats in a small space: juniper forest, meadow, scree, high snowfields and deep canyons carved by rivers with names like Aksu, meaning white water. Wildlife includes ibex, argali, brown bear, lynx and, in the high country, snow leopard, though your chances of seeing the cat are close to zero.

Spring is when the area earns its reputation. In April and May, the lower hills fill with wild tulips, including species that grew here long before the flower became a Dutch obsession, and meadows turn red, yellow and white for a short season. The Karabastau canyon has a collection of ancient rock carvings, and in the surrounding valleys you can find old burial mounds and other traces of the herders who lived here for millennia. Nearby, in the countryside around Zhabagly village, is a shrine to Arystan Bab, a revered teacher said to have taught Khoja Ahmed Yasawi.

The ride from Shymkent heads east on fast tarmac, then turns into the hills on narrower roads that pass farms, orchards and small villages. Corners become more frequent as the land rises, and the last stretch to the reserve can be bumpy and unpaved in places. Livestock roams freely, and in spring there is often mud. The air is clean and cooler than the plain, and the light on the snow peaks is often superb, particularly in the early morning.

You need to plan carefully. Entry into the reserve usually requires a permit, and it is easiest to arrange in advance through the reserve office or a local guesthouse. Fuel is not available near the reserve; Tyulkubas is the closest larger town, and Shymkent is the safe place to fill up completely. In the villages you will find simple guesthouses that serve warm bread, soup, honey and tea. Come in spring for the tulips, or in early autumn when the air is crisp and the hills turn gold.
